summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including under Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for all partners regardless of gender.

The absence of a ban carries no protective machinery. A stakeholder submission by Savie asbl and co-signatories to the country's 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review (March 2024) states that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights. The constitution has banned same-sex marriage since 2006, and there is no legal recognition of gender identity: a trans person cannot change legal gender documents. Queer In The World (updated 3 December 2023) likewise records no legal gender change and advises LGBT travellers to maintain discretion and a low profile.

Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under Article 176 of the Penal Code, which punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions, and local ordinances are applied against LGBTQ people. GayOut rates the country High Risk for LGBTQ+, noting that LGBT expression is censored and can expose a person to imprisonment. Enforcement is not statutory criminalisation but discretionary police and administrative action, so exposure depends on local conduct and official decisions rather than a fixed offence.

Physical violence is documented. Queer In The World reports violence, harassment and torture against LGBT people involving the police, security forces and the army. GayOut reports that armed militia groups in eastern DRC have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and that the collapse of state authority in parts of the country leaves legal protections theoretical. Church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral, contributing to an environment of social hostility.
tangentialFactors:
State violence and impunity extend beyond LGBT targeting and bear on visitor safety. Human Rights Watch (4 December 2017), drawing on more than 120 interviews including nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials and 21 M23 fighters, documented security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda between October and December 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi.

The safety picture differs by region. Eastern provinces carry the documented militia violence described in the sources, while national legal protections remain theoretical in areas where state authority has receded. A visitor's exposure therefore varies with where they are and which authority, if any, controls the area.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition and no relationship recognition: same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 2006. Same-sex conduct itself is legal and the age of consent is equal for everyone.

Domestic residents face police and security-force violence, harassment and torture as reported by Queer In The World, alongside censorship of LGBT expression and prosecutions for public same-sex affection under Article 176 and local ordinances. Local church organisations actively promote the position that homosexuality is immoral. A March 2024 stakeholder submission filed for the 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review records that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
The characterisation of enforcement rests on advocacy and travel-guide sources (Savie asbl UPR submission, Queer In The World, GayOut) rather than published Congolese court decisions; no conviction figures for Article 176 were available in the inventory, so the frequency of prosecution is unresolved.

Claims about militia violence against LGBTQ people in eastern DRC come from a travel-risk guide and are not corroborated here by incident-level reporting with dates and named victims. Whether Article 176 has been applied specifically to trans people, as distinct from LGBT people generally, is not sourced.

The Human Rights Watch documentation of M23 recruitment concerns protest suppression generally; its specific bearing on LGBT-directed violence is not established in the inventory, and it is presented here as context on state violence and impunity rather than as an LGBT finding.
